overview: Fletcher Building is New Zealand's largest vertically-integrated building materials, distribution and residential development group, dual-listed on the NZX and ASX (Foreign Exempt Listing). Following a strategic review completed in FY2025-26, the Group has simplified into a manufacturing- and distribution-led portfolio (Light Building Products, Heavy Building Materials, Distribution, Residential & Development) after classifying its loss-making Construction division as a discontinued operation from 31 December 2025 and completing its sale to VINCI Construction on 29 May 2026 (Tradelink was separately disposed 30 September 2024, and the smaller Fletcher Reinforcing and Wire business was sold to United Industries in April 2026 for NZ$15.7m at a flagged loss of up to NZ$23m). Core brands include GIB plasterboard, Laminex, PlaceMakers, Mico, Golden Bay Cement and Firth, with FY ending 30 June and operations concentrated in New Zealand plus a meaningful Australian manufacturing footprint.

business_model.summary: Fletcher Building manufactures and distributes building materials (plasterboard, insulation, laminates, steel, concrete, aggregates, pipes) largely sold through its own and third-party merchant networks, supplemented by a residential land/home development business. Revenue is transactional and tied to construction and renovation activity rather than recurring/subscription in nature; earnings are highly geared to residential and commercial construction volumes in New Zealand and, to a lesser extent, Australia. The now-divested Construction division was project-based infrastructure/vertical building work that repeatedly generated large loss provisions (NZICC, Puhoi-Warkworth) and has been exited as part of the turnaround; from 31 December 2025 it is reported as a discontinued operation, so continuing-operations figures (revenue $2,866m in 1H FY26; $5,644m restated FY2025) now represent the pure materials, distribution and residential business.

revenue_streams.name: Materials & Distribution (Light Building Products, Heavy Building Materials, Distribution)

business_model.customer_type: B2B trade/merchant and builder customers, plus B2C via retail-facing distribution (PlaceMakers, Mico) and direct residential home/land sales
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand ~75-80% of continuing revenue, Australia ~20-25% (Laminex, Iplex, Stramit, Fletcher Insulation); continuing-operations revenue was $5,644m in FY2025 (restated) and $2,866m in 1H FY26 (broadly flat vs $2,852m pcp); FY2025 total group revenue (incl. discontinued Construction) was $7,196m

main_competitors: James Hardie / USG Boral (plasterboard, fibre cement)
Holcim / Firth alternatives (Allied Concrete, cement importers)
New plasterboard entrants (import-based competitors challenging GIB's historic dominance)
competitive_position.market_position: Dominant #1 position in NZ plasterboard (GIB/Winstone Wallboards, ~94% share per Commerce Commission), cement (Golden Bay) and building products distribution (PlaceMakers); smaller, more fragmented positions in Australia (Laminex, Iplex, Stramit)

moat_factors.description: ~94% NZ plasterboard market share (Winstone Wallboards) built over decades of manufacturing and code-compliance systems, though now under active regulatory and competitive challenge
PlaceMakers/Mico branch networks provide reach and trade relationships that are costly to replicate, though margins are thin and competitive
Ownership across aggregates-cement-concrete and manufacturing-distribution chains provides some cost and supply security advantages
GIB, Laminex and PlaceMakers are trusted, code-specified brands in NZ construction

weaknesses: Repeated history of value destruction from capital-heavy, low-return Construction/infrastructure contracting (now exited but legacy liabilities remain)

GIB's dominant position is now a regulatory target (Commerce Commission Auckland High Court proceedings, filed Oct/Nov 2024, alleging retroactive rebate practices 2017-2022) and faces genuine new entrant competition for the first time in decades
High fixed-cost manufacturing base is highly operationally geared to the NZ construction cycle, which is currently subdued
Legacy quality/product liability issues (Iplex WA pipes) reflect broader execution and quality-control weaknesses
Balance sheet still carries above-target-midpoint net debt, constraining capital returns and strategic flexibility

growth_drivers: Cyclical recovery in NZ residential construction: building consents up ~19% YoY to over 40,000 in the year to June 2026, signalling a bottoming/early recovery in volumes feeding FY2027+ materials demand, though still well below the ~51,000 2022 peak

Portfolio simplification into higher-return manufacturing/distribution segments (Construction sold to VINCI; Fletcher Reinforcing and Wire sold to United Industries) and adoption of ROIC as the central value metric, aimed at re-rating the business away from historically low group ROIC

Cost-out programme: ~$200m gross cost savings delivered through FY25, plus ~$45m further YTD 1H FY26 savings in Warehouse/distribution and SG&A, with full-half benefits still to flow through in 2H FY26; head office headcount cut from 700+ to ~411

Balance sheet deleveraging (net debt cut from $1,766m Jun-24 to $999m Jun-25) freeing capacity for eventual dividend reinstatement once net debt reaches the lower half of the $400m-$900m target range; further ~$334m VINCI proceeds earmarked for FY27 debt paydown

Growth capex in core manufacturing (new Firth Auckland batching plant, Fletcher Insulation Sonata Acoustics facility, recycled aggregate expansion at Winstone Aggregates) to support market share and efficiency as volumes recover
Early signs of stabilisation in the Australian manufacturing businesses (Laminex, Stramit) after a prolonged downturn

Decentralised operating model giving Business Unit General Managers full accountability for operational performance, customer relationships and ROIC, intended to sharpen capital discipline across the simplified portfolio

business.description: Group earnings are highly geared to NZ (and to a lesser extent Australian) residential, commercial and civil construction volumes, which remain subdued; management (CEO Andrew Reding) says it is 'not forecasting great times' for FY26 and expects a more meaningful recovery only from calendar 2027
New entrants are challenging GIB's historic near-monopoly for the first time in decades, threatening the Group's highest-margin franchise

Even after divesting Construction to VINCI, Fletcher Building retains liabilities/risk on NZICC and other legacy vertical projects, including active SkyCity litigation over NZICC (NZICC reached Practical Completion and was handed over in Feb-2026), which the company says it will 'vigorously defend'

business.risk: Execution risk on new divisional structure
business.description: The 1 July 2025 reorganisation into Light Building Products/Heavy Building Materials/Distribution/Residential & Development, alongside the Construction exit and smaller divestments (Reinforcing and Wire), is a major operating model change still being embedded

financial.description: Pre-IFRS16 net debt was back up to ~$1,164m at Dec-2025 (from $999m at Jun-2025) due to residential land purchases, still above the midpoint of the $400m-$900m target range; company guided to be slightly above midpoint by 30 June 2026; dividends remain suspended until net debt is in the lower half of that range

FY2025 statutory EBIT was -$260m (vs. +$384m before Significant Items) on $644m (continuing + discontinued) of Significant Items (impairments, restructuring, Iplex WA provision); net losses attributable to shareholders were -$419m in FY2025 and a further -$11m in 1H FY26 (continuing-ops net earnings +$45m offset by -$56m discontinued-ops losses)
Meaningful Australian manufacturing revenue and costs create translation and transaction exposure

regulatory.risk: Commerce Commission proceedings against Winstone Wallboards (GIB)
regulatory.description: The Commerce Commission has filed Auckland High Court proceedings (Oct/Nov 2024) alleging Winstone Wallboards' retroactive tiered rebate arrangements with merchants (2017-2022) breached the Commerce Act (sections 27 and 36) by damaging competition and harming consumers via anti-competitive conduct; Winstone holds ~94% of the NZ wallboard market; case could take years to resolve and carries reputational, remedial and potential penalty risk

regulatory.risk: Iplex Australia WA 'Pro-fit' pipes matter - unresolved class action
regulatory.description: Despite the A$155m (NZ$170m) Industry Response provision and settlement finalised in June 2025, a separate Federal Court of Australia class action (commenced 5 August 2024, Baker McKenzie acting for claimants, case managed by Justice Button in the Victorian Registry) alleging Typlex-resin Pro-fit pipes are prone to crazing/cracking remains live and unresolved; the Court has ordered further discovery through 15-Dec-2025, 10-Apr-2026 and 8-Aug-2026, with no trial date yet set; potential for further provisioning beyond the Industry Response
Ongoing NZ government building consent and code reform could affect product specification requirements and competitive dynamics in plasterboard and other regulated materials

macro.description: After a period of rate cuts supporting the early consent recovery, reports in mid-2026 indicate the RBNZ has begun raising the OCR again, which could re-tighten mortgage rates and slow the nascent residential recovery
Below-average population growth and a large stock of unsold/available homes are cited as headwinds to new residential starts converting into completed, materials-consuming construction
Building costs have reportedly risen sharply on global cost pressures (e.g. geopolitical disruption), squeezing margins in a period of soft volumes and intense merchant competition

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ residential building consents rose ~19% YoY to over 40,000 in the year to June 2026 (still well below the 2022 peak of ~51,000), signalling an early-stage volume recovery that should flow through to materials demand from late 2026 into 2027; management guides to a more meaningful recovery only from calendar 2027. Australian conditions show early signs of stabilisation but remain uneven.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - Fletcher Building is a classic late-cycle, capital-intensive building materials/distribution business with high operating leverage to residential and commercial construction activity; historically the Group has swung from peak EBIT of several hundred million dollars to statutory losses within a few years, reflecting large fixed manufacturing costs against volatile volumes
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - mortgage rates and the RBNZ OCR path directly drive housing starts/consents and therefore the Group's core materials volumes; renewed OCR hikes reported in mid-2026 are a fresh headwind to the recovery thesis

recent_developments.event: FY26 full-year results scheduled for release 19 August 2026 (imminent, just after this analysis date), with an investor briefing the same day; FY2025 dividend remained nil, no interim dividend declared for 1H FY26

Fletcher Building raised FY26 continuing-operations EBIT before Significant Items guidance to $400m-$403m (from a lower prior range), including ~$52m from surplus property sales (notably the Laminex Cheltenham site); ex-property EBIT guided at $348m-$351m, ~3.6% above prior guidance midpoint, driven by stronger Light Building Materials procurement/productivity

Fletcher Building requested and secured withdrawal of its Moody's credit rating (effective 25 June 2026) after a string of asset sales reduced net debt, while continuing to target investment-grade balance sheet metrics; ~NZ$450m of net cash proceeds from divestments earmarked for debt reduction; Jefferies reinstated coverage at Buy with an NZ$4.00 target around this time

Sale of the Construction division (including Higgins civil contracting) to VINCI Construction completed on 29 May 2026, with the purchase price increased from $315.6m to ~$334m after Higgins signed additional Integrated Delivery Contracts; ~2,300 employees transferred with the division

Fletcher Building agreed to sell the smaller Fletcher Reinforcing and Wire business to United Industries for NZ$15.7m, flagging a loss on sale of up to NZ$23m, as part of continued portfolio simplification around ROIC

1H FY26 result: revenue from continuing operations $2,866m (broadly flat vs 1H FY25's $2,852m); EBIT from continuing operations before Significant Items of $145m; net earnings from continuing operations of $45m attributable to shareholders - the first positive continuing-operations result since June 2023; operating cash flow improved materially to $156m (vs $87m pcp); Construction division reclassified as a discontinued operation from 31 December 2025 pending divestment, resulting in a net loss attributable to shareholders of -$11m after -$56m of discontinued-operations losses; available liquidity ~$0.8bn plus a new $200m bank liquidity facility

NZ International Convention Centre (NZICC) reached Practical Completion and was handed over to SkyCity ahead of its formal opening; Fletcher Building retains legacy liabilities/risk on the project post-Construction sale and states it will 'vigorously defend' SkyCity's NZICC litigation

FY2025 result: statutory EBIT of -$260m (vs. +$384m before $644m of Significant Items); revenue down ~9% to $6,994m (continuing basis) / $7,196m total group; net loss attributable to shareholders of $419m; no FY25 dividend declared; A$155m (NZ$170m) Iplex Australia WA 'Pro-fit' pipes Industry Response provision finalised in June 2025

$700m capital raise completed (shares outstanding roughly doubled, ~783m to ~1,075m), with ~$680m net proceeds used to repay $511m bank debt and $169m USPP debt, materially strengthening the balance sheet ahead of the Construction exit

guidance.as_of: 9 July 2026 trading update (FY26 Q4 volumes & guidance upgrade)
guidance.fiscal_year: FY2026 (year ended 30 June 2026; results due 19 August 2026)

items.metric: EBIT from continuing operations before Significant Items
items.notes: Includes ~$52m from surplus property sales (largely Laminex Cheltenham site, Australia); raised from prior guidance on stronger Q4 core volumes and manufacturing productivity

items.metric: EBIT from continuing operations before Significant Items, excluding property sales
items.notes: ~3.6% above prior guidance midpoint; driven by Light Building Products favourable raw material procurement, manufacturing productivity gains and increased scrap usage

items.target: Within $400m-$900m target range, guided slightly above midpoint by June 2026
items.notes: Net debt was $1,164m pre-IFRS16 at Dec-2025 (up from $999m at Jun-2025) on residential land purchases; VINCI/Construction sale proceeds (~$334m) and other divestment proceeds (Reinforcing and Wire $15.7m) earmarked for further debt paydown in FY27

items.target: Full run-rate benefit of ~$45m 1H FY26 cost actions to be realised in 2H FY26
items.notes: Follows ~$200m gross cost savings delivered through FY25 as part of the turnaround programme; head office headcount reduced from 700+ to ~411

items.target: No dividend until net debt reaches lower half of $400m-$900m target range, at which point policy will be reset
items.notes: Analysts (Forsyth Barr) have suggested dividends may not resume until as late as FY2028, noting net debt of ~$1.05-1.15bn 'must halve', absent further asset sales accelerating deleveraging

guidance.management_commentary: Management (Chair Peter Crowley, CEO Andrew Reding) describe 1H FY26 as showing 'resilience' with 'solid progress in resetting the business' despite subdued NZ residential and civil markets and intense Distribution-division competition weighing on margins. Reding has said the Group is 'not forecasting great times for our financial year 2026,' and expects 'calendar year 2027 is when things are lined up and moving properly,' with 'a more meaningful recovery not anticipated until calendar year 2027.' Australia is showing 'early signs of stabilisation,' though conditions remain uneven. The July 2026 guidance upgrade reflects improving Q4 core volumes and productivity, but management continues to flag a softening commercial construction outlook alongside the residential recovery.

bull_case: Genuine self-help turnaround: portfolio simplified to higher-return manufacturing/distribution, Construction division (including chronic loss-maker Higgins/NZICC-style vertical projects) fully divested to VINCI, smaller non-core units (Reinforcing and Wire) also exited, $200m+ of structural cost-out delivered, and ROIC now the central internal value metric

Balance sheet materially de-risked - net debt cut roughly in half from the FY2024 peak, Moody's rating voluntarily withdrawn from a position of strength, ~$0.8bn of liquidity headroom, and further divestment proceeds (~$334m from VINCI) earmarked for additional deleveraging in FY27

First positive continuing-operations net earnings since June 2023 (1H FY26: $45m) and a raised FY26 EBIT guide ($400m-$403m) show the earnings trajectory has inflected positively even before a cyclical recovery is fully underway

NZ residential building consents up ~19% YoY to over 40,000 (year to June 2026) point to an early-cycle recovery in the core materials-intensive market that should progressively flow into FY27/28 volumes as a structural, understood housing shortage persists

Dominant NZ market positions (GIB plasterboard ~94% share, Golden Bay cement, PlaceMakers distribution) retain strong operating leverage to any recovery, and a dividend reinstatement (once net debt reaches target) would be a re-rating catalyst
bear_case: Structurally low returns and a long history of value destruction (NZICC, Puhoi-Warkworth, Iplex WA pipes, multiple divisional impairments) suggest execution risk remains elevated even after the Construction exit - large legacy liabilities (SkyCity NZICC litigation, unresolved Iplex Federal Court class action with discovery still running through August 2026) are still retained

The residential/commercial recovery management itself does not expect to be 'meaningful' until calendar 2027 ('not forecasting great times' for FY26), and reports of the RBNZ resuming OCR hikes in 2026 threaten to choke off the nascent consent recovery before it reaches completed-construction materials demand

GIB's historically dominant, high-margin plasterboard franchise (~94% NZ share) faces a live Commerce Commission Auckland High Court case alleging anti-competitive rebate conduct, plus genuine new entrant competition for the first time in decades - a structural margin risk to the Group's best asset

Net debt rose again in 1H FY26 (to $1,164m from $999m) on residential land purchases, still above the target-range midpoint, meaning no dividend is likely before FY2028 on some analyst models (Forsyth Barr), capping near-term shareholder returns

The stock has already re-rated substantially off its lows (roughly $2.65 to ~$3.81 over the past year, near its 52-week high of $3.97), with analyst price targets (Citi NZ$3.40-3.70 Neutral, Jefferies NZ$4.00 Buy) clustered close to or below the current price, so much of the self-help/turnaround narrative may already be priced in ahead of the 19 August 2026 FY26 result, leaving limited margin of safety if the cyclical recovery disappoints
